newsitem.title: UK: Elderly tankers to continue operating - report.
newsitem.headline: Elderly tankers to continue operating - report.

text.p: Oil tankers built in the 1970s are likely to remain in the fleet for several more years, confounding expectations that the vessels would be scrapped once they are 20 years old, a report said on Thursday.
The report, "World Tanker Outlook to 2010", published by Petroleum Economics Ltd, said tanker demand "is expected to continue to rise on the back of extremely buoyant growth in oil demand."

It said tanker demand would rise by 2.5 percent per year over the next 10 years and added, "This rate of demand growth is expected to significantly outstrip the rate of addition to the tanker fleet over the next three/four years."

"Therefore, it is likely to require a substantial proportion of tankers approaching 25 years old to remain in the fleet" even though these vessels had previously not been expected to operate beyond 20 years, the report said. However tankers would not have a lifespan of more than 30 years, it added.

"With scrapping limited to tankers which fail to meet current trading criteria (the consensus being that most of the poor quality tonnage has been scrapped), up to 70 percent of mid 1970's built tankers could continue to trade," the report said.
"However, even in this case, the tanker surplus is likely to continue to diminish through the end of the century."

The report said orders for new tankers were likely to rise by 1997/98, sparked by rising freight rates, and this would continue until a tanker surplus started to grow again, probably early in the next century.

"Although, after some 20 years of very poor trading conditions, the tanker industry has eliminated the 'structural surplus' which built up as a consequence of the oil supply crises of 1973 and 1979, there is no reason to expect the industry has eliminated the cyclical nature of the business," it added.
